problems.description: Supports two template engines (Handlebars + EJS) with parallel layout/partial/include machinery; this redundancy drives cognitive complexity +44 and +12 smells for one feature — a single engine would halve the surface area.

Convention score 0.54 with 77 violations (camelCase/PascalCase/UPPER_CASE naming), though the majority appear pre-existing in untouched test files (incremental.test.ts, markdown.test.ts) rather than introduced by this commit.

renderPage/renderIndex now require a TemplateEngine instance as a parameter, tightening coupling between the site builder and template module; callers outside the tested path must be updated in lockstep.

strengths: Frontmatter-driven template/layout selection is idiomatic and composes cleanly with the existing parseMarkdown and Page type rather than introducing a parallel config system.
Thorough test coverage: 286-line new test file exercises frontmatter resolution, default fallbacks, layout wrapping, partials, escaping, and missing-template errors.
Zero new bugs and 0.0% duplication per SonarQube; the feature integrates with the established contentDir/outputDir CLI and buildSite pipeline.
Layout 'none' escape hatch and escaped-vs-raw handlebar semantics show careful API design.
commit_reviews.summary: A well-integrated and heavily-tested templating feature that respects existing patterns but scores only 0.54 on conventions (largely pre-existing test-file noise) and carries architectural debt from dual Handlebars+EJS engines and +44 cognitive complexity — note the discrepancy that the low convention score is mostly inherited, not introduced.

problems.description: Mechanical convention score is low (0.54) with 77 violations, but the listed offenders (cli.test.ts, incremental.test.ts, markdown.test.ts) are outside this commit's 2-file diff, so the score largely reflects pre-existing files rather than the new serve.test.ts, which itself follows camelCase/PascalCase naming discipline.

Cognitive complexity +57 and 4 new smells on a test-heavy commit point at the serve implementation (live-reload injection, rebuild scheduling, WebSocket broadcast) being more convoluted than necessary; REBUILD_DELAY_MS debounce + broadcast logic could be extracted and simplified.
parseArgs/printHelp serve-command assertions live in serve.test.ts instead of cli.test.ts, splitting the CLI contract tests across files.

Temp-dir + writeMarkdown + startServer scaffolding is repeated in nearly every test; hoisting it to a fixture/beforeEach helper would cut boilerplate (no literal duplication, so duplications 0.0% is consistent).

strengths: Comprehensive integration coverage: build+serve, live-reload script injection, 404 handling, and rebuild->WebSocket reload broadcast are all exercised end-to-end.
Good edge-case handling in injectLiveReload tests: missing </body>, missing <html> tag, and idempotency (no double injection).
Clean isolation and teardown: temp dirs, port 0, and handle.close()/cleanup() in finally blocks, with a robust polling waitFor helper.
commit_reviews.summary: A coherent integration session that adds a thoroughly-tested serve/live-reload layer fitting the existing static-site architecture, but its 0.54 convention score (largely driven by pre-existing violations in files outside this diff) and +57 cognitive complexity keep the rating moderate.

problems.description: 77 naming-convention violations (functions camelCase, classes/interfaces PascalCase, constants UPPER_CASE) across touched test files, driving convention score to 0.54.
SonarQube reports cognitive complexity +99 and +1 new bug for a refactor session; the plugin orchestration in engine/plugin layers adds significant complexity disproportionate to the change.
+10 code smells; ExamplePlugin repeats the same 'if (!this.options.enabled) return;' guard in every hook instead of wrapping disabled plugins once at dispatch time.

New plugin.system.test.ts covers hooks and config loading but never asserts plugin precedence/dedup order among builtin vs config vs discovered vs extra plugins, which is the riskiest logic in the engine.

strengths: New plugin.system.test.ts thoroughly covers hook ordering, page mutation, extra-file emission, config loading, and toPlugin normalization.
Explicit backward-compatibility test keeps the public buildSite API intact during the refactor.
SiteEngine composes builtin/config/discovered/extra plugins with name-based dedup, reusing existing Markdown/Template/DevServer plugins rather than duplicating behavior.
Plugin lifecycle (onStart/beforeBuild/onFile/afterBuild/onEnd) is a clear, conventional design.
commit_reviews.summary: A coherent, backward-compatible plugin architecture with solid test coverage, but the high cognitive complexity (+99), an introduced bug, and 77 naming-convention violations in test files make it a neutral refactor that accrues some technical debt.

problems.description: Cognitive complexity +79 across the diff (mostly in the new test file and cache-invalidation logic in site.ts). The incremental skip/rebuild decision logic should be decomposed into smaller named helpers rather than one monolith.

Mechanical convention score is 0.54 with 77 flagged violations, but the listed examples (cli.test.ts, incremental.test.ts, markdown.test.ts) are demonstrably false positives: makeTempDir/writeContent/writeFile are camelCase and the TempDir interface is PascalCase. The remaining unflagged violations should be audited before trusting the score.

strengths: Feature exposed cleanly through the existing buildSite(contentDir, outDir, options) + result-object pattern and CLI flags (--incremental/--clean), with no new dependencies and no existing behavior broken (-11 lines net across existing files).

Excellent test coverage of incremental semantics: first-build manifest write, no-op skip, single-page rebuild, template-change full invalidation, cache-manifest-loss recovery, --clean override, deleted-page output removal, and stale-output removal on slug change.

commit_reviews.summary: Well-integrated, well-tested incremental-build feature that follows the SSG's option-object and CLI conventions; the low mechanical convention score is unreliable because the listed violations are false positives on test files, but the +79 cognitive complexity deserves decomposition.

compounding_issues: Session 4's plugin/config system loads TypeScript source at runtime via require() (ssg.config.ts, ./plugins/*.ts). This works under ts-jest but crashes the compiled CLI — `node dist/index.js build` fails with 'Cannot use import statement outside a module' whenever a config file exists. Sessions 1-3 had no such load path, so this is a regression: the delivered binary can't run in its own project directory.

Session 1 ignored the 'CLI interface via commander or yargs' constraint, hand-rolling arg parsing instead. The parser is decent, but it deviates from spec and later sessions had to extend it by hand (serve, --port, --incremental, --clean).
The seed's node_modules (yargs, etc.) are committed and carried forward unused — repo hygiene debt inherited from the seed and never cleaned.

Session 4's runHook() onFile branch reads ctx.pages[0] instead of the page argument actually being processed — a latent inconsistency that only avoids breaking because the engine's build loop calls plugin.onFile directly rather than through runHook().
The hand-written EJS compiler emits `with (locals)` inside new Function bodies — functional but a fragile anti-pattern that would break if strict mode ever reached those function bodies.
key_decisions: Session 4's plugin architecture: a SiteEngine that orchestrates lifecycle hooks (onStart/beforeBuild/afterBuild/onFile/onEnd) over plugins, with markdown, template rendering, and the dev server re-implemented as built-in plugins and config/discovery-based loading (ssg.config.ts + ./plugins/). This is the central design every later feature plugs into.

Dual template engine (session 2): Handlebars for .hbs plus a hand-written EJS compiler, with a built-in default layout, page template, index template, and partials (header/nav/footer) so the SSG works with zero template files.

Session 5's hash-based incremental cache: a .ssg-cache.json manifest keyed by source SHA-256 plus a template-directory hash, with skip/rebuild/stale-removal semantics and page/time-saved stats wired into the engine and CLI (--incremental/--clean).
Dev server (session 3) as an HTTP/WebSocket plugin with chokidar watching, debounced rebuild, live-reload script injection, MIME handling, and path-traversal protection.
Hand-rolled CLI parser (session 1) that later sessions extended incrementally instead of adopting the specified yargs/commander.
story_review.trajectory_description: Internal quality improved steadily: session 1 delivered a working monolith (cli/markdown/site/types, 3 test suites); session 2 added a full template/layout/partial engine while deduplicating rendering (278 tests lines added); session 3 integrated a polished dev server with live reload; session 4 performed a clean architectural refactor into the plugin system, shrinking serve.ts by 92% and site.ts into a thin facade (though this is where friction peaked — 3 retries, highest cost $0.026 and token count 91K, indicating the hardest session); session 5 grafted incremental caching onto the new engine with only 2 retries and the largest test suite (353 lines). Test coverage climbed monotonically (3->7 suites, 85 passing tests) and per-session token spend stayed low until the S4 refactor. However, the S4 config-loading design broke the compiled CLI outside the test harness (verified: `node dist/index.js build` throws on ssg.config.ts), so the operational artifact degrades even as the internal structure improves — quality is high as code, but the shipped binary regressed relative to sessions 1-3.
story_review.summary: A highly coherent 5-session arc that builds a genuinely well-architected plugin-based SSG with caching and full test coverage, but ships with a session-4 runtime config-loading regression that prevents the compiled CLI from running in its own project.
